To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cobinding of synthetic ligand and natural ligands can form a ligand link to a functionally important loop, and this ligand link synergistically affects the structure and function.

the binding of the synthetic ligand to PPARγ can push the natural ligands out of the ortho pocket to the Ω-loop region, and this ligand link to the Ω-loop can synergistically affect the function of PPAR.

cobinding of synthetic ligand to orthosteric pocket of PPARγ can push natural ligand (fatty acid) out of orthosteric pocket and onto a different ligand-binding site on the surface of the protein, and that this ‘ligand link‘ can synergistically affect the function of PPARgamma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular mechanisms of ligand binding to PPARγ.

the development of new ligands for PPARγ, the discovery of the mechanism of action of these ligands, and the application of this knowledge to the development of new therapeutic strategies for diabetes.
the structural basis of ligand binding to PPARγ, a nuclear receptor that is a key target for drug discovery.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
synthetic ligands can bind to nuclear receptors in a variety of ways, including orthosteric, allosteric, and cooperative binding modes, with the latter two being ligand link binding modes.
the binding of synthetic ligands to nuclear receptors can induce conformational changes in the receptors and can also induce the release of natural or endogenous compounds from their binding pockets.
the binding of a synthetic ligands can alter the affinity and binding mode of endogenous and natural ligands and that this can have important consequences in terms of receptor structure and function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the binding of synthetic ligand to PPARγ orthosteric site can displace endogenous fatty acid from the orthosteric site, and the displaced fatty acid binds to the Ω-loop to form a ligand link, which can affect PPARγ function.

the binding of a synthetic ligands to the orthostetic pocket of a nuclear receptor can push natural and/or endogenous ligands out of the orthosteric pocket to an alternate binding site near the Ω-loop.
the synthetic ligand and natural/endogenous PPARγ fatty acid ligands can cobind to the receptor and form a ligand link to the functionally important Ω-loop.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the orthosteric binding site of nuclear receptors can be used as a platform for the design of allosteric ligands that modulate receptor function.

the binding of a synthetic ligands to the orthostetic pocket of a nuclear receptor can have a significant impact on the conformational dynamics of the receptor and its ability to bind endogenous and natural ligands.
the binding mode of a ligand is not always fixed, but can be altered by a second ligand, and that the binding mode can be influenced by the cellular context.
